print.concept: print() shows text on the screen. Text must be inside quotes, and sep= and end= change what goes between and after the pieces.

example.code: print("Hi", "Chilaka", sep=", ", end="!\n")
example.note: sep= goes between the pieces, end= goes after the last one.

mistake.symptom: SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 1) (<string>, line 1)
mistake.fix: Close every quote you open. A missing closing quote is a SyntaxError.

variation.prompt: Print the words a b c joined by dashes.
variation.starter: # print a, b, c with dashes between

variables.concept: A variable is a name stuck to a value. Assigning again moves the name to a new value; a, b = b, a swaps two names at once.

example.code:
a = 3
b = 5
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
example.note: Python evaluates the right side first, so the swap needs no temp variable.

mistake.fix: A name must be assigned before it is used. Move the assignment above the print.

variation.prompt: Swap x and y, then print x and y.
variation.solution:
x = 1
y = 2
x, y = y, x
print(x, y)

types.concept: Every value has a type. / always gives a float, // divides and rounds down, and % gives the remainder.

mistake.symptom: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
mistake.fix: You cannot add text and a number. Convert first: int("5") + 3 or "5" + str(3).

variation.prompt: Print 17 divided by 5 rounded down, then the remainder, on one line.

input-math.concept: input() always returns text. Wrap it in int() or float() before doing maths.

example.code:
n = int(input())
print(n * 2)
example.note: The text '4' becomes the number 4, so n * 2 is 8.

mistake.fix: Without int(), '4' * 2 repeats the text and prints 44. Convert with int(input()).

variation.prompt: Read a number and print it plus ten.

fstring.concept: An f-string puts values inside text: f"{name} is {age}". Anything inside the braces is Python.

example.code:
name = "Chilaka"
age = 3
print(f"{name} is {age + 1} next year")
example.note: The braces can hold any expression, here age + 1.

mistake.fix: Without the leading f the braces print literally. Write f"Hi {name}".

variation.prompt: Given item and price, print: item costs price

name-error-bug.concept: Reading error messages is a skill: NameError means a name was used before it exists, usually a typo or a missing assignment.

example.note: The message names the exact word Python could not find.

mistake.fix: Compare the spelling of the name in the error with the one you assigned.

bool-compare.concept: == compares, = assigns. Comparisons give True or False, and and / or / not combine them.

example.code:
x = 5
print(x == 5, x > 7, x > 3 and x < 10)
example.note: Each comparison is a bool; and needs both sides True.

mistake.symptom: SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Maybe you meant '==' or ':=' instead of '='? (<string>, line 2)
mistake.fix: Use == to compare. A single = is assignment and is a SyntaxError inside if.

variation.prompt: Print True if n is between 1 and 10 inclusive.

ifelse.concept: if runs a block only when its condition is True; else runs when it is not. The block is the indented lines.

example.note: Indentation shows which lines belong to which branch.

mistake.symptom: IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 2 (<string>, line 3)
mistake.fix: The line after if must be indented, otherwise Python raises IndentationError.

variation.prompt: Print even if n is even, otherwise odd.

elif-chain.concept: elif adds more questions. Python checks top to bottom and stops at the first True one, so order matters.

example.note: 85 fails the first test and passes the second, so only B prints.

mistake.fix: The broader test is first, so 95 prints B and A is unreachable. Put the strictest test first.

variation.prompt: Print pass for 40 or more, otherwise fail.

truthy.concept: Empty things are falsy: 0, "", [], {} and None. Everything else is truthy, so if items: means 'if there is anything in items'.

example.code:
for v in [0, "", [], "a", 7]:
    print(bool(v), end=" ")
example.note: Only 'a' and 7 are truthy.

mistake.fix: Compare with the value you expect, or just write if name:. == True is almost never what you want.

wrong-door.concept: Conditions with and / or are easy to get wrong. Read each one out loud as a sentence.

example.code:
age, ticket = 20, False
print(age >= 18 and ticket)
example.note: and needs both parts to be True, so no ticket means False.

mistake.broken:
age, ticket = 20, False
print("in" if age >= 18 or ticket else "out")
mistake.fix: or let an adult in without a ticket. If both are required use and.

modulo-logic.concept: % gives the remainder, so n % 4 == 0 means divisible by 4. Combine tests with and / or and brackets.

example.note: 1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it is not a leap year.

mistake.fix: and binds tighter than or, so this groups wrongly. Add brackets to say what you mean.

variation.prompt: Print True if n is divisible by both 3 and 5.

while.concept: while repeats as long as its condition is True. Something inside the loop must change so the condition can become False.

example.code:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1
print("go")
example.note: n shrinks each time, so the loop ends.

mistake.broken:
n = 3
steps = 0
while n > 0 and steps < 4:
    steps += 1
print("n is still", n, "after", steps, "rounds")
mistake.fix: A loop that undoes its own progress never ends. Check that the variable moves toward the exit.

variation.prompt: Print 1 to 3 using while.

break-continue.concept: break leaves the loop at once. continue skips the rest of this round and starts the next one.

example.note: 1 is skipped and the loop stops at 3, so 0 and 2 print.

mistake.fix: After break the loop variable keeps its last value. Do not expect the loop to finish all rounds.

range-offbyone.concept: range(a, b) starts at a and stops before b. range(5) is 0 to 4, so the count is b - a.

example.code: print(list(range(2, 6)), list(range(0, 10, 3)))
example.note: The stop value is excluded. The third number is the step.

mistake.fix: range(1, 5) stops at 4. To include 5 write range(1, 6).

variation.prompt: Print the numbers 1 to 5 each on its own line.

accumulator.concept: An accumulator starts at a safe value (0 for sums, 1 for products) and grows inside a loop.

example.code:
total = 0
for p in [3, 4, 5]:
    total += p
print(total)
example.note: Start at 0 so the first add keeps the first number.

mistake.fix: total was never created. Set total = 0 before the loop.

variation.prompt: Print the sum of 1..4 with a loop.
variation.solution:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i
print(total)

endless-loop.concept: An endless loop usually means the loop variable is never updated, or is updated the wrong way.

example.code:
n = 0
while n < 3:
    n += 1
print(n)
example.note: n += 1 moves toward the stop condition.

mistake.fix: Counting down while testing < 3 never finishes. Move toward the exit, not away.

nested-loops.concept: A loop inside a loop runs the inner one fully for every step of the outer one. Great for rows and columns.

example.code:
for r in range(1, 4):
    print("*" * r)
example.note: Row r prints r stars, giving a growing triangle.

mistake.fix: The inner loop prints on a new line each time. Use end=" " and a print() after the inner loop for a grid.

variation.prompt: Print a 3 by 3 block of # characters.

str-methods.concept: Strings have methods: upper(), lower(), strip(), title(), replace(). They return a NEW string.

example.code:
s = "  hello parrot "
print(s.strip().title())
example.note: strip() removes the outer spaces, title() capitalises each word.

mistake.fix: Methods do not change the original. Assign the result: s = s.upper().

variation.prompt: Print the word 'quiet' in capitals followed by !

str-index.concept: Strings are numbered from 0. s[0] is the first letter, s[-1] the last, s[a:b] a slice, and s[::-1] reversed.

example.note: Slices stop before the end index.

mistake.symptom: IndexError: string index out of range
mistake.fix: A word of 6 letters has indexes 0 to 5. Use s[-1] for the last letter.

variation.prompt: Print the first and last letters of 'Chilaka' together.

str-immutable.concept: Strings cannot be edited in place. To change one, build a new string from slices and methods.

example.code:
s = "cat"
s = "b" + s[1:]
print(s)
example.note: We made a new string 'bat' and moved the name s to it.

mistake.symptom: TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
mistake.fix: Item assignment on a string is a TypeError. Build a new one instead.

str-format.concept: Format numbers inside f-strings with a spec: {x:.2f} for two decimals, {n:>5} to right-align, {n:,} for thousands.

example.note: The part after the colon says how to show the value.

mistake.symptom: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "float") to str
mistake.fix: A float cannot be glued to text with +. Use f"Total: {price}".

str-search.concept: Use in to test membership and a loop or sum() to count: sum(c in 'aeiou' for c in word).

example.code:
w = "banana"
print(sum(c in "aeiou" for c in w), "n" in w)
example.note: The generator makes True/False per letter, and sum counts the Trues.

mistake.fix: count is case sensitive: 'B' is not 'b'. Use w.lower().count("b").

variation.prompt: Print how many times 'a' appears in 'banana'.

split-join.concept: split() turns text into a list of words, join() glues a list back into text. They are opposites.

example.code:
words = "a b c".split()
print(words, "-".join(words))
example.note: join is called on the separator, not on the list.

mistake.fix: join belongs to the string: "-".join(["a", "b"]).

list-basics.concept: A list holds ordered items. append adds one, remove deletes one, len counts, and indexes start at 0.

example.code:
bag = ["map"]
bag.append("rope")
bag.remove("map")
print(bag, len(bag))
example.note: append and remove change the list itself.

mistake.symptom: IndexError: list index out of range
mistake.fix: A one-item list only has index 0. IndexError means you asked for a place that is not there.

variation.prompt: Make a list of 3 fruits and print how many there are.

list-slice.concept: Lists slice like strings: xs[1:3], xs[:2], xs[-2:]. A slice is a new list.

example.note: Start is included, end is not.

mistake.symptom: IndexError: list index out of range
mistake.fix: Slices forgive going past the end, but a single index does not.

alias.concept: b = a does not copy a list. Both names point at the same list, so changing one changes the other. Use a.copy() for a real copy.

example.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
c = a.copy()
c.append(9)
print(a)
example.note: a changed through b, but not through the copy c.

mistake.broken:
a = [1]
b = a
b.append(2)
print("a is", a)
mistake.fix: If you wanted a separate list write b = a.copy().

dict-basics.concept: A dict maps keys to values: d["key"] reads, d["key"] = v writes, d.get("key", default) is the safe read.

example.note: get returns the default instead of crashing.

mistake.fix: A missing key raises KeyError. Use d.get("jam", 0) or check with in first.

variation.prompt: Print the price of 'milk' from the dict.

dict-iter.concept: Loop over a dict with .items() to get key and value together. A plain loop gives only the keys.

example.note: items() yields pairs which unpack into k and v.

mistake.symptom: ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)
mistake.fix: Looping a dict gives keys only, so unpacking fails. Add .items().

sets.concept: A set keeps only unique items and has no order. set(xs) removes duplicates quickly.

example.code:
xs = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3]
print(sorted(set(xs)), len(set(xs)))
example.note: sorted(...) gives a tidy list back.

mistake.fix: Sets have no positions. Convert with list(s) if you need an index.

variation.prompt: Print how many different letters are in 'banana'.

counting.concept: Counting with a dict: d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1. collections.Counter does it for you.

example.code:
from collections import Counter
print(Counter("banana").most_common(1))
example.note: most_common(1) gives the top pair.

mistake.fix: The key does not exist on the first visit. Use d.get(w, 0) + 1.

variation.prompt: Count the words in 'a b a' and print the count for 'a'.
variation.solution:
from collections import Counter
print(Counter("a b a".split())["a"])

comprehension.concept: A list comprehension builds a list in one line: [x * x for x in xs if x > 0].

example.code: print([x * x for x in range(5) if x % 2 == 0])
example.note: Read it as: x squared, for each x in range, if x is even.

mistake.broken: print([x * x for x in range(3) if x > 1 else 0])
mistake.fix: The if filter goes at the end with no else. For a choice use x*x if cond else 0 at the front.

variation.prompt: Print the list of doubles of 1 to 4.

treasure-bug.concept: When data goes missing, print what you have at each step. The bug is usually where the value changes unexpectedly.

example.code:
items = ["map", "key"]
found = [i for i in items if i == "key"]
print(found)
example.note: A filter keeps only matching items; if it matches nothing you get [].

mistake.broken:
items = ["map", "key"]
print([i for i in items if i == "Key"])
mistake.fix: Case matters. Compare lower() on both sides.

def-basics.concept: def names a reusable recipe. return hands a value back; print only shows it.

example.note: double(4) is 8, so we can keep calculating.

mistake.symptom: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'
mistake.fix: print shows 8 but returns None, and None + 1 is a TypeError. Use return.

variation.prompt: Write area(w, h) that returns w times h.
variation.solution:
def area(w, h):
    return w * h

args-default.concept: Parameters can have defaults: def hi(name="friend"). Never use a list as a default, it is shared between calls.

example.note: The default is used when you pass nothing.

mistake.broken:
def add(x, bag=[]):
    bag.append(x)
    return bag
print(add(1), add(2))
mistake.fix: The same list is reused, so the second call also holds 1. Use bag=None and create the list inside.

variation.prompt: Write hi(name='friend') returning 'Hi ' plus the name.

return-none.concept: A function without return gives back None. If your result is None, look for a missing return.

example.note: The sum is computed and thrown away.

mistake.symptom: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for *: 'NoneType' and 'int'
mistake.fix: None * 2 is a TypeError. Add return x + 1.

scope.concept: Names made inside a function stay inside it. Pass values in with parameters and out with return.

example.code:
x = 1
def f():
    x = 2
    return x
print(f(), x)
example.note: The inner x is a different name, the outer x stays 1.

mistake.fix: y only exists inside f. Return it instead.

star-args.concept: *args collects extra positional values into a tuple, **kwargs collects extra named ones into a dict.

example.note: Positional extras go to a, named extras to k.

mistake.symptom: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'list'
mistake.fix: Passing one list makes nums hold a list inside a tuple. Call total(*[1, 2, 3]) or total(1, 2, 3).

variation.prompt: Write total(*nums) that returns the sum.

recursion.concept: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem and needs a base case that stops it.

example.note: fact(5) = 5 * fact(4) = ... down to fact(1).

mistake.fix: No base case means it never stops: RecursionError.

variation.prompt: Write fib(n): fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, then the sum of the two before.

toolkit.concept: Small helper functions that each do one thing can be combined into bigger tools.

example.note: words reuses clean, so the logic lives in one place.

mistake.fix: clean returns None because the return is missing.

try-except.concept: try runs risky code; except catches a named error so the program can carry on.

example.note: The bad conversion jumps straight to the except block.

mistake.symptom: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
mistake.fix: ValueError stops the program. Wrap the conversion in try/except ValueError.

variation.prompt: Write safe_int(s) returning the int or 0 if s is not a number.

finally.concept: finally always runs, error or not. Use it to clean up.

example.code:
try:
    print(1 / 1)
finally:
    print("done")
example.note: Even on success the finally block runs last.

mistake.fix: Without except the error crashes the program, but finally would still run first.

raise.concept: raise stops the function with an error you choose, which is how you reject bad input.

example.note: The message you wrote comes back in the except block.

mistake.fix: Raise with a helpful message: raise ValueError("age must be 0 or more").

files.concept: Use with open(name, 'w') to write and 'r' to read. with closes the file for you, and read().splitlines() gives the lines.

example.code:
import os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "ak_demo.txt")
with open(p, "w") as f:
    f.write("a\nb\n")
with open(p) as f:
    print(len(f.read().splitlines()))
example.note: Two lines were written, two lines are read.

mistake.symptom: FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/nonexistent/x.txt'
mistake.fix: FileNotFoundError means the path is wrong. Check the folder and the spelling.

csv-data.concept: Split each line on commas to get columns: name, score = line.split(","). Convert numbers with int().

example.code:
line = "Ravi,42"
name, score = line.split(",")
print(name, int(score) + 1)
example.note: Both pieces come out as text, so score needs int().

mistake.symptom: ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
mistake.fix: Three pieces cannot go into two names: ValueError. Check how many columns the line has.

json-data.concept: json.dumps turns data into text and json.loads turns it back. Keys come back as strings.

example.code:
import json
s = json.dumps({"a": [1, 2]})
print(s, json.loads(s)["a"][1])
example.note: A round trip returns the same data.

mistake.symptom: JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)
mistake.fix: JSON needs double quotes. Single quotes are invalid and raise JSONDecodeError.

crashing-counter.concept: Crashes often come from assuming input is clean. Guard the risky line instead of the whole program.

example.note: Only the division is guarded.

mistake.fix: ZeroDivisionError: decide what the answer should be when b is 0.

debug-print.concept: To find a bug, print the values at each step and compare them with what you expected.

example.code:
xs = [2, 4, 6]
total = sum(xs)
print("total", total, "count", len(xs))
print(total / len(xs))
example.note: Printing both numbers shows the average is 12/3.

mistake.fix: The divisor is a typed number, not len(xs). Use len so it works for any list.

modules.concept: import gives you tools others wrote. import random, then random.randint(1, 6). Seed it to repeat results.

example.code:
import random
random.seed(7)
rolls = [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(3)]
print(all(1 <= r <= 6 for r in rolls))
example.note: Whatever the rolls are, each is between 1 and 6.

mistake.fix: NameError: math was never imported. Add import math at the top.

shadow.concept: If you name a variable max or list you hide the built-in of that name. Pick other names.

example.code:
nums = [3, 9, 4]
biggest = max(nums)
print(biggest)
example.note: Using biggest keeps max usable.

mistake.fix: max now holds 5, which cannot be called. Rename the variable.

traceback.concept: A traceback reads bottom to top: the last line is the error, the lines above show where it happened.

example.note: The last line names the error and why.

mistake.fix: IndexError: pop from empty list. Check that the list has items first.

dates.concept: datetime.date does calendar maths: subtracting two dates gives a timedelta with .days.

example.code:
from datetime import date
print((date(2026, 3, 1) - date(2026, 2, 1)).days)
example.note: February 2026 has 28 days.

mistake.symptom: ValueError: day is out of range for month
mistake.fix: That date does not exist: ValueError. Check the month length.

class-basics.concept: A class bundles data and actions. __init__ sets up each new object and self means 'this object'.

example.note: Each Dog remembers its own name through self.

mistake.fix: Without self.name the value is thrown away. Write self.name = name.

variation.prompt: Write class Box with a count attribute set to 0.

class-shared.concept: A value defined on the class is shared by every object; a value set on self belongs to one object.

example.code:
class A:
    items = []
a, b = A(), A()
a.items.append(1)
print(b.items)
example.note: Both objects use the same list.

mistake.broken:
class A:
    items = []
a, b = A(), A()
a.items.append(1)
print(len(b.items))
mistake.fix: Put the list in __init__ as self.items = [] so each object has its own.

inherit.concept: A child class gets everything from its parent. super() calls the parent's version so you can extend it.

example.note: Cat reuses Pet and adds to it.

mistake.fix: Cat.__init__ forgot to call super().__init__(n), so n was never set.

dunder.concept: Special methods like __str__ and __eq__ let your objects work with print and ==.

example.note: print calls __str__ to get the text.

mistake.fix: Two separate objects are never equal unless you define __eq__.

typehints.concept: Type hints like def f(n: int) -> str document what goes in and out. Python does not enforce them, but tools and readers love them.

example.note: The hints say: takes an int, returns a str.

mistake.fix: The hint says str but we returned an int. Hints are promises you must keep yourself.

early-return.concept: Guard clauses return early for bad cases so the main logic stays flat and readable.

example.note: The special case leaves first.

mistake.fix: If no branch returns, the function falls off the end and gives None.

mutable-arg.concept: A function that changes the list you pass in changes your original. Return a new list when you can.

example.code:
def add(xs):
    return xs + [9]
a = [1]
print(add(a), a)
example.note: xs + [9] makes a new list, so a is untouched.

mistake.broken:
def add(xs):
    xs.append(9)
a = [1]
add(a)
print(a)
mistake.fix: append changed the caller's list. Copy first or return a new one.

clean-code.concept: Clean code uses clear names, one job per function, a docstring, and assert for quick self-checks.

example.code:
def area(w, h):
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return w * h
assert area(2, 3) == 6
print("ok")
example.note: If the assert were wrong the program would stop with AssertionError.

mistake.fix: A failing assert shows that your belief is wrong. Fix the code or the expectation.

big-o.concept: Count how many steps grow with the input: one loop is about n steps, a loop in a loop about n times n.

example.note: 4 by 4 gives 16 steps.

mistake.broken:
xs = list(range(5))
print(sum(1 for a in xs for b in xs))
mistake.fix: Doubling n quadruples this count, which is why nested loops get slow.

search.concept: Linear search checks every item. Binary search needs a sorted list and halves the range each time.

example.note: Each round throws away half of the list.

mistake.broken:
xs = [1, 3, 5]
lo, hi = 0, 2
while lo < hi:
    lo = lo
    break
print("never moved")
mistake.fix: If lo and hi never change the search loops forever or ends wrong. Always move one bound.

pairs.concept: Sorting two words makes anagrams equal; a dict or set remembers what you have seen so a pair can be found in one pass.

example.note: Both tricks avoid comparing everything with everything.

mistake.fix: Capital letters sort before lowercase. Use .lower() before comparing.

cli.concept: argparse turns command line words into variables with --flags and help text.

example.code:
import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=1)
print(p.parse_args(["--n", "3"]).n)
example.note: The type= converts the text to a number.

mistake.broken:
import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--n")
print(p.parse_args(["--n", "3"]).n + 1)
mistake.symptom: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
mistake.fix: Without type=int the value stays text, so adding 1 fails. Add type=int.

pipeline.concept: A log pipeline reads lines, filters them, then counts: each stage does one small thing.

example.code:
lines = ["ok a", "ERR b", "ok c", "ERR d"]
errs = [l for l in lines if l.startswith("ERR")]
print(len(errs))
example.note: Filter first, then count.

mistake.broken:
lines = ["ok a", "err b"]
print(len([l for l in lines if l.startswith("ERR")]))
mistake.fix: Case matters: 'err' does not match 'ERR'. Normalise with .upper() first.

html-scrape.concept: HTML is text with tags. To scrape, find the tag text between markers, then convert it to the type you need.

example.code: html = "Rs 42" price = int(html.split("Rs ")[1].split("<")[0]) print(price + 1)
example.note: Two splits isolate the number, int() makes it a number.

mistake.symptom: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
mistake.fix: The piece still has '' and is text, so + 1 fails. Cut at '<' and use int().

regex.concept: A regular expression describes a text pattern. re.findall returns every match: \d+ means one or more digits.

example.code:
import re
print(re.findall(r"\d+", "a1 b22 c333"))
example.note: Each run of digits is one match.

mistake.fix: A single \d matches one digit at a time. Add + to match a whole run of digits: \d+.

api-json.concept: An API reply is JSON text: parse it, then pick keys. Guard for missing keys with .get().

example.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"temp": 31, "city": "Hyd"}')
print(d["city"], d.get("rain", 0))
example.note: get supplies a default when the key is absent.

mistake.fix: A missing key is a KeyError. Use d.get("rain", 0).
